title: A KING WAS SO HUMILIATED BY A WOMAN THAT HE ASKED HIS SERVANT TO KILL HIM
paragraphs: A KING WAS SO HUMILIATED BY A WOMAN THAT HE ASKED HIS SERVANT TO KILL HIM
He murdered his brothers to seize power. He burned people alive to keep it. But in the end, one unnamed woman standing above him shattered the reputation he was desperately trying to save.
There are deaths in the Bible that make you grieve.
There are deaths that make you tremble.
And then there are deaths that read like warnings carved into stone.
Abimelech’s was one of them.
He had spent his life reaching upward.
Up toward power.
Up toward recognition.
Up toward a throne he was never meant to possess through bloodshed.
But when his story finally ended, he was not standing above a kingdom.
He was lying beneath a tower.
Bleeding.
Broken.
His skull crushed by something dropped from the hands of a woman whose name Scripture does not even tell us.
And even then…
even with death closing in…
even after violence had brought him to the ground…
Abimelech was still worried about what people would say about him.
That may be the most frightening part of the story.
Because some people would rather control the story told about their death than surrender the life they still have to God.
Judges 9:53–54 records the moment:
“וַתַּשְׁלֵךְ אִשָּׁה אַחַת פֶּלַח רֶכֶב עַל־רֹאשׁ אֲבִימֶלֶךְ וַתָּרִץ אֶת־גֻּלְגָּלְתּוֹ”
The Hebrew describes a woman throwing an upper millstone upon Abimelech’s head and crushing his skull.
Then comes the detail that exposes what was still alive inside him even as his body was dying.
He urgently called the young man carrying his weapons and told him, in essence:
“Draw your sword and kill me, so they cannot say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’”
And his armor-bearer thrust him through.
Abimelech died.
But before we rush past that scene, we need to understand how he got underneath that tower.
Because nobody suddenly becomes Abimelech in Judges 9:54.
The man beneath the millstone had been forming for years.

Abimelech was a son of Gideon, also called Jerubbaal. After Gideon died, Abimelech went to his mother’s relatives in Shechem and appealed to blood loyalty. He essentially asked them whether they would rather be ruled by Gideon’s many sons or by one man who was their own flesh and blood.
The men of Shechem listened.
Money was taken from the temple of Baal-berith.
Abimelech used it to hire reckless men.
Then came the horror.
Judges 9 tells us that Abimelech went to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his brothers—seventy sons of Jerubbaal—“on one stone.”
One survived.
Jotham.
Imagine the silence after that slaughter.
Brothers who had grown up together.
Men with names.
Memories.
Mothers.
Stories.
Futures.
Gone.
And what was Abimelech reaching for through all that blood?
Power.
He wanted to be king.
There is something terrifying about ambition when it becomes more precious than obedience.
There is something deadly about the human heart when it begins saying:
“I deserve this.”
“I need this.”
“I cannot let anyone stand in my way.”
“I have come too far to turn back now.”
That voice does not always begin with murder.
Sometimes it begins much smaller.
A lie you refuse to confess.
A relationship you know dishonors Christ but will not surrender.
A secret addiction protected behind passwords and deleted histories.
A bitterness you keep feeding because forgiveness feels too much like losing.
A ministry that slowly becomes more about being seen than seeing Jesus glorified.
A reputation you polish publicly while your private life collapses.
A hunger to win every argument.
A desperate need to prove people wrong.
A refusal to apologize because admitting guilt would wound your pride.
That is why Abimelech’s story should not merely make us stare at him.
It should make us examine ourselves.
Because sin rarely walks into your life announcing where it intends to take you.
It whispers.
Just this once.
Nobody needs to know.
You deserve it.
Protect yourself.
Protect your image.
Protect your position.
Do whatever it takes.
Then one compromise becomes another.
And another.
Until one day you discover that the thing you thought you controlled has been controlling you.
Abimelech reached the throne.
But getting what you desperately wanted is not always evidence that God approved the way you got it.
That sentence may hurt somebody reading this.
Because we live in a world that loves visible success.
Numbers.
Money.
Influence.
Titles.
Platforms.
Applause.
People assume that if something grew, God must have blessed it.
If somebody became powerful, God must have favored him.
If the door opened, God must have opened it.
Scripture is far less naive.
Abimelech became king.
And Abimelech was still under judgment.

Jotham had already spoken a prophetic warning against Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem. In his parable, the trees sought a king, and eventually the bramble accepted the position, declaring that if the trees truly wanted it to reign, they should take refuge beneath its shadow—but otherwise fire would come from the bramble.
The warning was devastating.
And eventually the alliance built around Abimelech began consuming itself.
Judges 9:23 says God sent an evil spirit—or a harmful spirit—between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and their relationship fractured.
The conspiracy that helped establish him became part of the environment that destroyed him.
The violence he used to climb upward eventually came back downward.
And this is where the story becomes almost unbearable in its symmetry.
Abimelech had killed his brothers on a stone.
Abimelech would eventually be struck down by a stone.
He had used violence to establish his name.
Now he was dying while desperately trying to protect that name.
He had climbed over bodies for power.
Now his own body was collapsing beneath a tower.
Judges does not leave the meaning of his death for us to invent.
It tells us.
“Thus God returned the evil of Abimelech, which he committed against his father in killing his seventy brothers.”
That is Judges 9:56.
This was judgment.
Not random bad luck.
Not merely battlefield misfortune.
Not simply an embarrassing military accident.
Scripture interprets the event morally.
God was bringing Abimelech’s evil back upon him.
But there is another detail that should stop us cold.
When the millstone struck him, Abimelech apparently understood that he was dying.
He had only moments.
Maybe seconds.
And what mattered to him?
His reputation.
“Lest they say of me, ‘A woman killed him.’”
Think about that.
His skull was crushed.
Death was approaching.
His kingdom could not save him.
His power could not save him.
His soldiers could not save him.
His reputation could not save him.
Yet reputation was still what occupied his mind.
He wanted control over the final sentence.
He could not control death anymore.
So he tried to control the obituary.
And thousands of years later, the irony is devastating.
His plan failed.
Because Scripture still tells us exactly what he did not want people saying.
A woman brought him down.
In fact, generations later, when David sent Uriah into danger, Joab anticipated David’s anger over soldiers approaching too close to a wall. He told the messenger to remind David of Abimelech:
“Who struck Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth? Did not a woman cast an upper millstone upon him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez?”
That is recorded in 2 Samuel 11:21.
The reputation Abimelech tried to erase became the reputation history remembered.
Pride promised him control.
Pride could not even control one sentence after his death.
And maybe that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
How much of your life is being spent trying to control what people think about you?
How many things have you refused to confess because somebody might look at you differently?
How many tears have you swallowed because you need everyone to believe you are strong?
How many times have you said, “I’m okay,” when your soul was screaming?
How much sin survives because exposure feels more frightening than bondage?
Some people are not afraid of sin anymore.
They are afraid of being caught.
There is a difference.
Some are not heartbroken that they betrayed God.
They are heartbroken that somebody discovered it.
Some do not want repentance.
They want reputation management.
And the Gospel will not merely renovate your reputation.
Jesus came to resurrect dead hearts.
That is where Abimelech’s story forces us toward a question far bigger than Abimelech.
What do you do when the truth about you is ugly?
What do you do when you cannot rewrite your own past?
What do you do with the scandal?
The affair.
The addiction.
The rage.
The years wasted.
The secret messages.
The hypocrisy.
The selfishness.
The pride.
The betrayal.
The things nobody knows.
The things everybody knows.
The thing you would give anything to undo.
You can spend the rest of your life protecting your image.
Or you can bring the truth into the light of Jesus Christ.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christianity does not teach that you save yourself by becoming better at hiding your scandal.
Christianity announces that the sinless Son of God came for sinners.
Jesus did not need reputation management.
He needed no cover story.
He committed no sin.
Yet He willingly entered our shame.
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Stripped.
Crucified.
And unlike Abimelech, Jesus did not use another man’s weapon to escape humiliation.
He endured the cross.
Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus endured the cross, “despising the shame,” and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
The King of kings willingly endured public shame to rescue people drowning in private shame.
Do you see the contrast?
Abimelech was willing to die differently so people would speak differently about him.
Jesus was willing to die publicly so sinners could become different through Him.
Abimelech clung to reputation.
Jesus embraced the cross.
Abimelech spilled the blood of his brothers to gain a kingdom.
Jesus shed His own blood to redeem brothers and sisters for His Kingdom.
Abimelech destroyed others to exalt himself.
Christ humbled Himself to save others.
One king shows us what pride does when given power.
The true King shows us what holy love does with power.
Jesus Christ is not merely another character in the story of humanity.
He is the Savior toward whom our desperate need points.
And perhaps you are reading this while carrying something you have tried desperately to hide.
You know exactly what it is.
Nobody had to name it.
Your mind went there before your eyes reached this sentence.
You have become skilled at changing the subject inside your own soul.
You worship.
You smile.
You post Scripture.
You encourage other people.
You say “God is good.”
And He is.
But somewhere behind all of that is a locked room you keep hoping Jesus will not ask you to open.
He already knows what is inside.
And He is still calling you.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Not because judgment is imaginary.
Abimelech’s story should destroy that illusion.
But because the Gospel announces something Abimelech never understood:
You do not have to protect a false version of yourself when grace offers you a new life.
Repentance is not humiliation without hope.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.

The Greek word commonly translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν—homologōmen—from the idea of acknowledging or agreeing. Biblical confession is not negotiating with God about whether our sin was really sin.
It is coming into agreement with the truth.
“Yes, Lord.”
“It was sin.”
“I did it.”
“I cannot cleanse myself.”
“I need mercy.”
“I need Christ.”
That is radically different from Abimelech.
His dying concern was essentially:
Do not let them remember me this way.
Grace invites you to say:
Jesus, You already know me completely. Save me anyway.
And He does not save repentant sinners because they deserve another chance.
He saves because Christ is sufficient.
The cross is sufficient.
His blood is sufficient.
His resurrection is sufficient.
His grace is sufficient.
There is no sinless person reading this article.
Romans 3:23 says all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
But the story does not end at Romans 3:23.
Romans 6:23 tells us that although the wages of sin is death, the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That means your scandal does not have to become your final identity.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Your failure does not become your savior, and neither does your success.
Jesus does.
This does not mean earthly consequences magically disappear.
Forgiveness does not make evil harmless.
Grace does not turn repentance into an excuse.
Sometimes wounds must be repaired.
Sometimes trust must be rebuilt.
Sometimes consequences remain.
But in Christ, condemnation does not get the final word over the redeemed.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
That is 2 Corinthians 5:17.
The Gospel does not say:
Hide better.
It says:
Come into the light.
The Gospel does not say:
Save your reputation.
It says:
Lose your life for Christ and find it.
The Gospel does not say:
Rewrite your own story until people admire you.
It says:
Surrender your story to the One who raises the dead.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you have been living like Abimelech in one quiet way.
Not murdering brothers.
Not conquering cities.
But protecting the image.
Terrified of being known.
Terrified of confession.
Terrified that if people saw the real battle behind the profile picture, the church clothes, the family photos, the ministry position, the laughter, they would leave.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse hiding with healing.
They are not the same thing.
A wound hidden beneath clothing is still a wound.
A chain covered by religious language is still a chain.
A secret sin decorated with excuses is still sin.
And Jesus loves you too much to call darkness light.
He calls you out because He calls you home.
Repent.
Turn.
Confess.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop trying to write an ending where everyone thinks you were stronger than you really were.
You were never meant to be your own savior.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, comment, “no more hiding.”
Not because strangers need your private details.
They do not.
You do not need to publicly disclose sensitive sins to prove repentance.
But perhaps those three words can become a line in the sand between pretending and surrender.
No more hiding.
If your spirit is exhausted and you need believers to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has already been restoring parts of your life you once thought were beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not become their prosecutor.
Pray for them.
We have enough spectators.
The Church needs brothers and sisters willing to carry one another toward Jesus.
Not because every sentence will feel comfortable tomorrow.
Not as a superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Send it to the believer who has drifted.
The person ashamed to return to church.
The friend who thinks God could never forgive what they have done.
The family member who needs Jesus.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely about pretending to be good.
Let them discover that the Gospel is actually for people who finally admit they are not.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin, understand grace, and keep your eyes on Jesus Christ, follow and stay close.
Do it as support for Gospel work, not as a transaction with God.
You cannot purchase God’s blessing.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot earn heaven by supporting a ministry.
But if this work genuinely glorifies Christ and serves people with biblical truth, voluntarily supporting it is one practical way you can help that work continue and reach others.
Come to Jesus.
Not to us.
Not to a platform.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a religious image.
Jesus.
Because one day, every reputation we spent years constructing will become irrelevant.
The applause will stop.
The followers will move on.
The titles will belong to somebody else.
Our carefully managed public identities will disappear.
And what will matter is not whether we successfully convinced the world that we were good.
What will matter is whether we belonged to Christ.
Abimelech spent his final breath trying to protect his name.
Do not spend your life doing the same.
Let them know you needed mercy.
Let them know you were a sinner rescued by grace.
Let them know there were chapters you are ashamed of but a Savior you are not ashamed of.
Let them know Jesus found you in the wreckage.
Let them know repentance was painful but freedom was worth it.
Let them know your scars did not disappear overnight, but Christ taught you they no longer had to define you.
Let them know you stopped hiding.
And when people ask how someone with your past can still have hope…
tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them about the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Tell them that grace is not permission to remain who you were.
Grace is the miracle that means, through Christ, you do not have to.
Abimelech desperately wanted history to remember a different sentence about his death.
You still have time to surrender the sentence being written by your life.
Do not die protecting the version of yourself Jesus came to crucify and make new.
